title: Detecting Accounting Fraud in Publicly Traded U.S. Firms Using Machine Learning Approach

scopes.description: Complete supplied workflow: transcribe and configure the SAS preparation embedded in the PDF, then run the supplied MATLAB RUSBoost28 script and its reader/evaluation helpers after resolving the SAS-to-MATLAB input contract. Preserve pooled SAS construction and winsorization plus the 2003–2008 RUSBoost analysis.

requirements.description: WRDS/Compustat annual industrial firm-year source consumed as fraud.compustatindustrial7815. The actual SAS code requires source variables used in joins, filters, formulas and the 28 raw features. It filters fyear to 1978–2015 before lag construction, then winsorizes the full retained pooled population at the 1st/99th percentiles; the datasheet separately reports fiscal years 1991–2014 for the accounting data in the paper’s current version. Keep these as the supplied construction and later analysis windows, respectively.

issues.description: The substantive SAS preparation is embedded in a PDF and begins by reading fraud library tables. No standalone .sas driver, libname/import setup, input file paths, working directory, or output directory is supplied. This is a preparation/configuration gap; the supplied formulas and macro should be preserved in a working copy.

The environment inventory records a SAS 9.4 startup failure during TKELS initialization. Runtime availability is unverified; this is not evidence of a missing license and no additional SAS startup attempt was made.

The SAS program ends by creating fraud.all after a selected KEEP and a raw Compustat join; no CSV export to the MATLAB input is present. The frozen MATLAB reader requires 37 positional columns: year, firm, sic, insbank, understatement, options, paaer, new_paaer, label, then 28 features. The SAS output code does not establish the options or new_p_aaer columns or a 37-column export order. The current author repository lists data_FraudDetection_JAR2020.csv, whose current reader contract has 32 positions (year, firm, p_aaer, label, 28 features) and whose current runner uses 300 trees and test years 2003–2014; it is not a demonstrated compatible replacement for this supplied RUSBoost28 branch (3,000 trees, 2003–2008, new_p_aaer). Request the exact matching prepared file/version or author field mapping; do not guess aliases or change the target analysis.

The supplied helper files are named 20191108 data_reader.m and 20191108 evaluate.m, but declare functions data_reader and evaluate, which the runner calls by those bare names. Resolve names in a working copy so MATLAB can find the functions; retain original bytes and do not change their contents. The runner itself is a script stored under a date-prefixed name with a space and can also be staged under a conventional working-copy name.

The MATLAB command was not found on the inherited PATH, and the exact MATLAB Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox functions required by the supplied branch have not been checked in an available MATLAB session. Actual installation/version/toolbox entitlement remains unknown.

The SAS program reads fraud.compustatindustrial7815 directly, but the supplied PDF does not show how that exact table is produced from the catalog-listed COMP.FUNDA file or how its industrial membership/population is formed. The local COMP.FUNDA candidate has the required variable names and is readable in a one-row probe, but its catalog label and sampled fyear=1961 row do not establish an industrial filter, the retained 1978–2015 panel, or the lag/history and pooled-winsorization population. Keep the local file as a candidate, not a verified substitute or proof of absent licensing.

The included winsor macro obtains requested percentile cut points with PROC UNIVARIATE.
The supplied macro is called with byvar=none, type=winsor and 1st/99th percentile cut points on the derived features.
SAS selects variables into temp, joins that table to the raw Compustat table for additional analysis, sorts, and creates fraud.all; no CSV export is present in the supplied code.
Local MATLAB reader consumes CSV after its header and maps the uscecchini28 format positionally to fields through column 37.
Local runner fixes RNG seed, uses 3,000 RUSBoost iterations and a two-year gap, tests each year 2003–2008, and recodes overlapping serial fraud IDs in training labels.
Local code trains RUSBoost with a 5-observation leaf tree, learning rate .1, class ratio [1 1], predicts fraud probabilities, and evaluates at top one percent.

Datasheet says archival data came mainly from commercial sources, identifies the 1991–2014 Compustat period, and dates the extract to April 2017.
evidence.quote:
Archival data are used in this paper. The data are mainly obtained from commercially available sources.
The details are as follows.
    1) AAER Data: our initial accounting fraud sample comes from the SEC’s Accounting and Auditing
       Enforcement Releases (AAERs), as compiled by the University of California-Berkeley’s Center
       for Financial Reporting and Management (CFRM).
    2) The AAER database used in the current version of our paper includes all the AAERs announced
       over the period between May 17th, 1982 and September 30th, 2016. Since the CFRM has not
       updated the AAER database since 2017, we also hand collected additional fraud observations from
       the SEC website: https://www.sec.gov/divisions/enforce/friactions/friactions2018.shtml that are
       dated up to December 31, 2018 (AAER #4012). We make the fraud observations available (see
       item 5)
    3) Financial Accounting Data: The publicly traded U.S. firms’ accounting data are from
       COMPUSTAT fundamental annual database fiscal year 1991 to 2014. The data from
       COMPUSTATA used in the current version of the paper were downloaded in April 2017.

evidence.description: Datasheet explicitly describes the packaged AAER_firm_year file, SAS preparation, and the label content of the CSV, so the historic CFRM purchase is not automatically a present-day data barrier.
evidence.quote:
The fraud firm years observations, SAS and Matlab programs used in this paper are publicly available on
JAR online supplements and datasheet webpage (https://research.chicagobooth.edu/arc/journal-of-
accounting-research/online-supplements).
The file “AAER_firm_year” contains both the initial fraud firm years from CFRM and additional fraud
firm years of AAERs announced after September 30, 2016 up to December 31, 2018 by hand-collection.
The file “SAS coding” shows the process of merging fraud firm years with COMPUSTATA database and
prepare necessary accounting features for our prediction models.

evidence.description: Local datasheet names the earlier uscecchini28.csv prepared dataset, misstate label, 28 raw feature names, and new_p_aaer serial-fraud identifier.
evidence.quote:
We also made the final dataset                       publicly     available     in    our     Github     repository
(https://github.com/JarFraud/FraudDetection).
The file “uscecchini28.csv” is our final dataset which contains the fraud labels and feature variables. The
variable name of our fraud label is “misstate” (1 denotes fraud, and 0 denotes non-fraud). The variable
names of the 28 raw financial data items are: act, ap, at, ceq, che, cogs, csho, dlc, dltis, dltt, dp, ib, invt,
ivao, ivst, lct, lt, ni, ppegt, pstk, re, rect, sale, sstk, txp, txt, xint, prcc_f. The variable name of 14 financial
ratios are: dch_wc, ch_rsst, dch_rec, dch_inv, soft_assets, ch_cs, ch_cm, ch_roa, issue, bm, dpi, reoa, EBIT,
ch_fcf. The variable new_p_aaer is used for identifying serial frauds as described in Section 3.3 (see the
code in “RUSBoost28.m” for more details).
